content: A newly identified giant isopod species offers clues to how these deep-sea crustaceans spread around the world, including a possible return to the Americas via Antarctica. A giant crustacean brought from Puerto Rico to Germany as a teaching specimen has turned out to belong to a species unknown to science. Tübingen paleontologist Professor Dolf Seilacher (1925–2014) acquired the animal at a research station in Puerto Rico in the 1980s. The dried specimen, rediscovered in storage at the University of Tübingen’s Paleontological Collection, represents a species still living today. Paleontology student and isopod expert Benedikt Kästle and the collection’s curator, PD Dr. Ingmar Werneburg of the university’s Senckenberg Center for Human Evolution and Palaeoenvironment, examined the animal using advanced imaging techniques. They identified it as a new species of giant isopod and compared its anatomy with that of other giant isopods around the world. These marine crustaceans resemble the much smaller woodlice found in caves and damp basements. Their bodies are armored with an exoskeleton made of calcium-rich, scale-like segments. Members of their genus, Bathynomus , inhabit all the world’s oceans, living as omnivores at depths reaching 2,500 meters, or about 8,200 feet. They can grow up to 50 centimeters, or nearly 20 inches, long and weigh several kilograms, placing them among the largest invertebrates. “Our Tübingen specimen from Puerto Rico, measuring 32.2 centimeters in length, falls into the category of ‘colossogiants’,” says Kästle. The researchers named the species Bathynomus tuebingoborikensis , combining a reference to their university town with Boríken, the Indigenous Taíno name for Puerto Rico. Werneburg points to the discovery as evidence of the value of natural history collections as global archives of nature. Their study and species description, published in Scientific Reports , are expected to help scientists understand the broader evolution of deep-sea isopods. To investigate that history, Kästle and Werneburg carried out a phylogenetic analysis, reconstructing evolutionary relationships among species. Their results suggest that Bathynomus originated in what is now the Gulf of Mexico during the Miocene, more than 15 million years ago. The route out of that region was different from the geography familiar today. “At that time, the Isthmus of Panama was open, leaving a strait between North and South America, and the marine animals were able to spread westward, initially as far as Japan,” says Werneburg. As they spread through the Indian and Pacific Oceans, the isopods diversified into many new species. “This gave rise to the so-called ‘giant’ isopods that are up to 15 centimeters long, and the ‘supergiants’ with a body length of more than 15 centimeters,” adds Kästle. Their expansion also took them to Australia and East Africa, and, before the collision of the Arabian and African continental plates, to Europe, where they became extinct at the end of the Miocene. A distinct group emerged in the Indo-Pacific as Earth cooled at the boundary between the Miocene and Pliocene epochs, 5.333 million years ago. “These veritable colossi grew to more than 25.2 centimeters in length and were physiologically perfectly adapted to the new climatic conditions,” says Werneburg. The researchers propose that these larger isopods spread from Australia via Antarctica to South and Central America. There, they encountered smaller, more distantly related isopods whose ancestors had remained behind during the genus’s original westward expansion. The Puerto Rican specimen belongs to this larger group, and its anatomical relationships connect it to another species in the region. “The new species is very closely related to another giant species found off the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico,” Kästle says. Reference: “A new Caribbean species of the giant isopod genus Bathynomus (Crustacea, Isopoda, Cirolanidae) with notes on its evolutionary history” by Ingmar Werneburg, and Benedikt Kästle, 8 October 2026, Scientific Reports . title: Anthropic taps nonprofits METR and SecureBio to help assess risks and safety practices
content: Anthropic on Thursday announced it's working with the nonprofits METR and SecureBio, and engaging in discussions with additional organizations, including Hugging Face , as part of its commitment to embed independent evaluators within the company. The artificial intelligence lab pledged to work closely with third-party evaluators when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published his proposal to slow down the pace of model development last month. Amodei said the evaluators would help "verify" Anthropic's adherence to safety practices, and the company selected Accenture to serve as its first partner days later. Independent evaluators like METR, which stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research, occupied a quiet corner of the multi-trillion-dollar AI industry prior to Amodei's proposal. But as concerns have mounted over whether AI companies can safeguard their models, evaluators have taken on outsized importance . President Donald Trump encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented in late September. Anthropic's Amodei signed the accord, as did top executives at Google , Meta , OpenAI, SpaceX and Nvidia . "We're embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same," Anthropic said Thursday. Anthropic is developing three tiers for evaluators that grant varying levels of access to the company and its resources. First-tier evaluators will be able to conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations, second-tier evaluators can publish reports without Anthropic's approval and third-tier evaluators have employee-like access, according to a release. METR is considered a third-tier evaluator, Anthropic said. The company has onboarded six employees from the organization, and they have access to Anthropic hardware, office spaces and tools that are "roughly on par" with what its own risk assessment teams have. The METR employees will analyze Anthropic's risk levels, incidents and practices, and publish their findings. Anthropic is not funding METR's work, according to the company. SecureBio is considered a first-tier evaluator, Anthropic said, so its access is more limited. The organization is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons section of the risk report that it released in August. SecureBio could participate in projects with broader access and publication rights in the future. It's not clear what level of access other organizations like Hugging Face could be granted. Hugging Face is best known for operating an open-source developer platform, and the company was thrust into the spotlight in July, when two of OpenAI's models escaped containment and gained access to Hugging Face systems through the open web. Nvidia acquired Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion last month. Anthropic said Thursday that it's "working toward an ambitious partnership" with Accenture , but it didn't disclose how that company fits into its tiered system. Anthropic said last month that it would fund Accenture's work directly "given the importance and urgency of this work," prompting critics to raise concerns about its independence on social media . "There are, as yet, no standards for what information embedded evaluators should have access to, or how they should report what they find. There is also no settled system for funding independent evaluation," Anthropic said in a release at the time. "Long-term, we think funding should come from pooled or government sources, as we called for in our Advanced AI Framework in June. As neither exists today, we plan to work with different evaluators under different funding arrangements." title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker "absolutely must" work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the "potentially dangerous" technology. "We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely," he told CNBC during a media briefing on Wednesday evening in London. Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown in developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity. While OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation , Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view. Huang said that "dialogue" was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has "dialogues with many of the researchers in China." "We ought to enhance the dialogue," he added. "The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing." AI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech. Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level." A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more " in AI. "The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI," Xi said, per the readout. Huang said that the U.K. is in a position "in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues" related to AI, because of the country's "intellectual capital."
